title: The arrow-maker who didn't look up
hookLine: a wandering sage names his twenty-four teachers, and one is an arrow-maker who never noticed a king go by; Patanjali's remedy for the obstacles is that kind of attention
carry: eka tattva: one thing, returned to
tomorrow: a prince walks through a dazzling hall and leaves burning. what was missing?
last: NINE OBSTACLES, ALL PART OF THE PATH.

lines: A WHOLE PROCESSION. HE NEVER LOOKED UP.
cards: In the Bhagavata Purana, King Yadu meets a wandering sage, carefree and glowing, and asks where he found his peace. The sage, whom tradition identifies as Dattatreya, says: from twenty-four teachers.

The earth, the wind, the ocean, a moth, a honeybee, a python. One of them was an arrow-maker. The sage watched him at work, straightening an arrow, while a king's whole procession went by with all its noise and banners.

teach.h: THE PARADE CAN'T PULL IT AWAY.
teach.b: That, the sage says, is how the mind should rest on the Self: so gathered on one thing that the parade can't pull it away. Patanjali's remedy for the nine obstacles is the same.
Sutra 1.32: tat pratishedhartham eka tattva abhyasah. To ward them off, practice on one principle. Eka, one.
Tattva, a principle, literally thatness. Abhyasa, the steady return. Which one thing?
The commentators part ways. Vyasa reads it as any single object the mind is fixed on; others point back to the sutras on Ishvara and om. Both share a shape: stop spreading out.
The obstacles feed on scattering. Doubt grows when you keep switching methods; plateaus feel endless when you keep starting over somewhere new.
Vyasa calls the gathered mind ekagra, one-pointed, the ground where real absorption becomes possible.
This is the teaching behind a very Hindu habit: keeping one ishta devata, one chosen form of God, and often one mantra received from a teacher, for years, sometimes for life.

Not because the other forms are false; Hindus honor many. One is simply where you dig. Today, it's choosing one practice and keeping it long enough to work, while the parade of new apps and new methods goes by.

how: Many Hindus keep one ishta devata, a chosen form of God, and one mantra, often received from a teacher, for years rather than switching, and teachers often cite Yoga Sutra 1.32 or the arrow-maker of the Bhagavata for this.

o: a calm mind once the obstacles are gone
a mind moving freely among many objects
one-pointed: a mind resting on a single object

p: one-pointed: a mind on a single object

s: Patanjali gives a separate cure for each of the nine obstacles
sutra 1.32 gives one remedy: practice on one principle.
commentators disagree about what the one principle is
Vyasa reads any single object; others read it as Ishvara, from the sutras just before.
the arrow-maker in the Bhagavata stopped to watch the king's procession
he was so absorbed in his arrow that the whole procession passed unnoticed.

games.q: you've said one mantra for a month. a friend swears by another, and there's a new meditation app. what does sutra 1.32 suggest?
o: stay with the one you have and keep returning to it.
games.why: to ward off the obstacles, practice on one principle. switching keeps the mind scattered, which is what the obstacles feed on; it is why many Hindus keep one ishta devata and one mantra.

practice: Choose one thing for this sit: the name of your chosen form of God if you pray, or the breath at the nostrils, or the feel of your hands resting.

Each time the mind offers a second thing, a better object, a plan, a new technique, let it pass like the king's procession, and come back to the one you chose. Don't switch, even when something else looks more interesting.

wordCard.voice: Ekagra, one-pointed, a mind fixed on a single object, like the arrow-maker at his work. Sutra 1.32: to keep the obstacles away, practice on one principle, returning to it again and again.

orig.note: Sanskrit ekāgra: one-pointed, a mind fixed on a single object. Vyasa's term; the source of 'one-pointed'.

carryVoice: Your line: eka tattva, one thing, returned to. The arrow-maker didn't look up. Day four hundred thirty-nine, done.
